speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 181, to amend the National Harbours Board Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
In presenting the resolution in connection with the present bill I referred to the growth since 1935 of traffic and earnings of our national harbours. Hon. members will perhaps be interested in a few figures to illustrate the increase in business of our harbours under the administration of the national harbours board.
In 1953 the number of vessels entering national harbours was almost 50,000, in contrast with 32,000 in 1935. Total cargo tonnage in 1953 was 42,500,000 tons as compared with 24,500,000 tons in 1935. Total revenues increased from $7,400,000 in 1935 to $21,000,000 in 1953.
As I have already pointed out, this growth in traffic and earnings has been accompanied by an increase in the responsibilities of the board. It is the view of the government that an increase in the membership of the board would enable its members to make more frequent visits to the ports under its administration.
I am sure it is not necessary for me to emphasize the desirability of close contact between the members of the board and various local organizations such as shipping bodies, boards of trade and municipal councils of the communities served by our national harbours. Personally, I would like to see these contacts develop in an increasing degree as I am firmly convinced that there is everything to be gained by consultation with local interests. A larger board can, I think, carry out this policy without impairing its head office administration and consideration of over-all policy.
Lest there be any thought that the costs of administration of the national harbours board are top-heavy, may I say that in his national ports survey, 1931-32, Sir Alexander Gibb estimated the annual cost of a central harbour

board at $200,000. In 1953, more than 20 years later, the actual head office expenses of the national harbours board amounted to $213,000, which includes $23,000 for a staff of the comptroller of the treasury. Having regard to the decline in the purchasing power of the dollar in the interval, I am sure hon. members will agree that head office expenses are by no means out of line with the amount originally considered reasonable.
For these reasons I would urge the house to give second reading to this bill forthwith.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the suggestion of the minister with respect to the connection between the national board and the local organizations in the various port cities of Canada is one which I am sure will meet with the approval of all hon. members. On reading the speech of the minister the other night, on the resolution stage of this bill, I was somewhat intrigued when I thought, perhaps erroneously, that the minister was questioning the advisability or the desirability of local advisory councils or committees. If I followed him correctly this afternoon, he emphasized the importance of having a four-member board which will be active, which will travel and which will establish contacts, as he said, with local boards of trade and with other organizations in the various cities throughout Canada. I would suggest to him, sir, that if that premise is correct-and I think it is-then there is all the more reason why the minister should welcome the creation of local committees or local advisory councils, as Sir Alexander Gibb recommended years ago, with which organizations those members of the board can consult, meet and work together in the interest of the port.
In speaking on this matter the other night on the resolution stage, as reported at page 1513 of Hansard, the minister said this:
My own inclination, Mr. Chairman, is to believe that with an active membership on the board itself the advantages of local advisory committees can be attained through this greater activity on the part of the members of the board without running into some of the disadvantages.
When the minister closes this debate, I hope he will explain what are the disadvantages of these local committees or advisory councils on which the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) spoke at some length and with some emphasis the other night, and which are included in the report of Sir Alexander Gibb. I know that in Halifax we have had operating for som* considerable time the port of Halifax commission, which is a body incorporated by the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia, and which includes within its membership, management, [DOT]epresenting shipping interests, labour-for 50433-109J
National Harbours Board Act instance, the president of the stevedoring union is a member of that commission- representatives of the provincial government and representatives of the municipality as well as of the public at large.
I am suggesting to the minister, sir, that this commission has accomplished a great deal of good. I would suggest that it is in keeping with the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra the other night and also in keeping with the recommendation in the Gibb report of many years ago.
The minister referred to the increased activity of those four members. I do not know whether he is suggesting that heretofore they have been inactive. I doubt very much whether they have. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat intrigued by this fact. For almost a year and a half- as I recall it, from 1951 until some time in 1952-one member of this national harbours board had retired and the government saw fit to have the board operate with two members. We at least can welcome the fact that they have now recognized the importance of this board and the membership is being increased.
I am suggesting that four members operating from Ottawa, no matter how fast they travel or where they go, will not be able to maintain the local contacts and to build up the efficiency of the ports in the same way as can be done through local commissions. Take the situation in Halifax for a moment. You have there, as I said, the president of the stevedoring union, a member of the commission. He in turn, of course, is in direct contact daily with his stevedores, and everyone knows that some of the many troubles which arise in ports are due to labour conditions and the suggestions of inefficiency, and so forth, between the unions and the shipping interests. That has been largely outdated in the city of Halifax. The unions have been brought into the field with their representatives on the port commission. They work in close conjunction with management, with shipping agents, with shipping owners and with the authorities of Halifax and the representatives of the province and city. We have not an ideal situation, of course. One never gets ideal situations in this mundane sphere, but it is a situation which I think is a relatively happy one and one which should be copied and emulated in other parts of Canada. It is true that in other cities-for instance, in the city of Quebec-they have a committee of some kind. I understand that Montreal has not; but the point is that in the Gibb report great emphasis was laid on the matter of local advisory councils. I am

National Harbours Board Act suggesting at any rate that the experience of my own province and of that port, which plays no insignificant part in the national economy of this country, one which is often referred to as "the warden of the honour of the north", is such that we have established a pattern which I suggest does not support what I took to be a rather critical view by the minister when he said that he thought that the activities of these four members would be such as to overcome what he termed the disadvantages of these local committees. There certainly is room for activity on the part of these committees.
Personally I am glad to see that the board is to be enlarged and strengthened as there are many things which I think it should be doing. I would hope that the board will now be able to study more closely the shipment of Canadian goods through Canadian ports, a matter about which we in the east feel most keenly and in connection with which I think we have fallen down very badly during the last few years. I am not going to take up the time of the house to put on the record figures which I have used at other times, but they are in keeping with the whole approach to the problem of our national harbours.
In connection with the administration of the harbours board I suggest to the minister that now we are going to have four members more attention should be paid to the development of business through our ports. I do not know whether it is correct, but I have been told that the situation in this regard has been improved somewhat during the last couple of years. There are many meetings held in Canada having to do with traffic matters. For instance, there is the international traffic authority, the international trade association, the Toronto exhibition and others. I am told that the port authority of New York, the port authority of Philadelphia and the railroads of the United States are represented at these meetings by their publicity agents.
These people are able to do much in the way of working up business and generally diverting traffic through United States ports and over United States railroads at the expense of our own. Now that there is to be an additional member on the board I would hope that the minister will see that more facilities are provided so that the members of the board may be able to travel, not only locally, important as that may be, but in order to attend these meetings. Another one that comes to my mind is the industrial traffic league of Canada made up of traffic men from


the North American continent. I submit that our national harbours board should be represented at these meetings.
I feel that this enlargement of the board will provide sufficient scope and opportunity for service in operating directly from the offices here in Ottawa and influencing trade as a whole. Of course the members should and will travel. The individual members will meet people in the different parts of Canada, but I reiterate that they cannot do this work properly by going down like a member of parliament making a sudden call on his political committee and then going away and thinking that everything is all right. We know that you have to go back again and again, and the same thing applies to the harbour commissioner. No one is naive enough to think that even by travelling you can make sufficient local contacts to enable you to deal with the development of a port and all those other problems which could be dealt with by a local committee.
I say again that I rose in this debate because I felt that the minister had suggested that there were obvious disadvantages in these local committees. I hope that when he closes his debate he will deal with this matter at length. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and others from this side of the house have suggested, I hope that in the scheme which he envisions with respect to the national harbours board greater emphasis will be laid upon decentralization, perhaps not of control but of personnel and personal contacts, something which has not been possible during the past years.

Mr. Speaker, I only wish to say a few words on the second reading of this bill. I was not in the house a week ago when it was considered in the resolution stage, but I have glanced over that debate and I wish to refer to a few of the points which were raised at that time.
This group will support this bill. The national harbours board of Canada is today big business. Without being able to offer any expert opinion on the matter, I feel that an additional member on the board is quite justified. This is a large country and if members of the board are going to keep themselves informed about the various harbours they will undoubtedly have to travel.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) suggested last Friday that as there is to be a fourth member appointed the new member should come from the Pacific coast. Without doubt Vancouver is one of the most important harbours in Canada. I do not wish to reflect upon any other section

of the country when I say that the Pacific coast province is the fastest growing province in Canada at the moment, and before many years go by Vancouver will be Canada's greatest port.
If my recollection of what I read in Hansard is correct, I believe the minister said that when members are appointed to a national board they become nationally minded regardless of the locality from which they may be chosen. I agree with the minister and I think that that is a good thing indeed.

I followed with interest the words of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) in connection with the port of Halifax commission. I clearly remember the representations made by people interested in the future of the port of Halifax over a number of years in connection with some form of local board or commission that would have the interests of the port at heart and which would be in a position to assist the national harbours board in the discharge of its duty relating to the port of Halifax. I believe that an excellent solution was found in the formation of the Halifax port commission which arose out of local initiative.
For a number of years there had been repeated requests that the government or the national harbours board set up some sort of local board. That was countered with the suggestion that with appropriate local initiative a board or commission of this nature could be constituted and the national harbours board and the Department of Transport would be only too pleased to co-operate with it. That suggestion was taken up and acted upon. The result is the port of Halifax commission which has been operating for several years.
I realize that we were very fortunate in the personnel that were selected to act on this commission. They were men of considerable experience with local matters and in connection with port operations particularly and they have done an excellent job in carrying out their responsibilities.
I also know that the port commission is very appreciative of the co-operation which it has received from the national harbours board. I think, all in all, this has proved

National Harbours Board Act to be an excellent development and a good experiment and it will continue to bring about good results in the future.
As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings suggested, this is perhaps not an ideal arrangement. I do not think any arrangement could be properly described as ideal. However, it has I think, worked well and to the advantage of the port of Halifax. It also has been useful to the national harbours board in their dealings with the port and in their attempts to make the kind of decisions that will be to the long-range advantage of the port.
I think it also should be pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that in addition to dealing with the national harbours board and in addition to taking an interest in the development of new facilities and improved equipment in the port, the port of Halifax commission has followed an excellent program of disseminating information and publicity about the port of Halifax and the facilities which it offers to shippers in Canada and to shippers from outside of Canada who wish to send goods into Canada. The commission publishes a regular bulletin which is widely distributed and which lists all the expected arrivals and departures of cargo and passenger ships to and from the port of Halifax. This information is provided so that those who wish to make arrangements to send cargo can have, in convenient form, up to date information on the freight space available into and out of the port of Halifax. I think this is a valuable service. It is a service which I believe the harbour board could not be expected to supply in the same way for every port. It is the kind of service that a local commission such as the port of Halifax commission can supply both effectively and usefully.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings referred to the problem of endeavouring to ensure that the greatest possible volume of Canada's foreign trade moves through Canadian ports. That end is being served by the port of Halifax commission through the activities which I have described.
One of the arguments which used to be presented by some shippers when they were approached in connection with this subject was that they had some difficulty in finding convenient cargo space from Canadian ports. Today none of them can give that excuse in so far as the port of Halifax is concerned because up to date and reliable information is provided in the way I have described.
The national harbours board, from a national point of view, has a responsibility in this connection, of course. I think that some improvement can and will be achieved in regard to that matter. However, in saying


that, I do want to say as well that the board does maintain a traffic department which has the responsibility of trying to ensure that Canadian goods are routed through Canadian ports. I have followed the activities of that traffic department since I have been in this house and I know that the activities and the efficiency of that department have been very materially improved during that time. I do not think this occasion should be missed to express our appreciation of the improvements which have been achieved and to express our hope that further effective action will be undertaken.
The volume of all types of cargo through the Atlantic ports, and particularly through the port of Halifax, has shown a gratifying increase last year over that of the year before and so far this year over that of last year. The activities of the port of Halifax commission and the traffic department of the national harbours board have both contributed to this welcome development. I am sure that both these agencies will continue to operate as they have in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I think there would be reasonably general agreement on the advantage of an extra member to the national harbours board. However, in the discussion on the resolution and again in the minister's explanation today I think it was evident that there were some large areas in which explanation might well have been given to this house concerning the appointment of this additional member of the board.
The national harbours board operate a vast amount of valuable real estate in Canada, worth approximately a quarter of a billion dollars, and they operate a business whose consolidated revenue is some $20 million a year. This house must therefore have more than a passing interest in the operation which comes under the direction of these gentlemen. We have had expressed by the minister the idea that, in his opinion, the appointment of this additional member will enable the board to make more frequent contact with localities, and to travel more widely; and implicit in all his remarks has been the suggestion that the appointment of the additional member would enable the board to do a much better job. Having read the minister's remarks and having listened today with considerable interest, I would also go as far as to feel that there was some reservation about the job currently being done by the national harbours board, that reservation being contained in the minister's remarks. That is my impression. I am not attempting to put words into his mouth, but that is certainly the impression I received.

I do not think that the appointment of an additional member is going to erase the type of problem which the minister, in his various remarks in connection with this bill, seemed to admit exists. The basic problem which affects many of our ports across the country is the lack of local knowledge and the lack of liaison between the local operation and the headquarters at Ottawa. We must admit immediately that in the operating branch there is liaison between the port manager and the board at Ottawa. But there are many other things which affect a port in addition to the operation. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) pointed out just a little while ago, there is the entire question of the future of that port, and that matter falls largely outside the field of operation.
In discussing this particular point here, Mr. Speaker, we are at a disadvantage because the minister has brought down this bill just before the report of the national harbours board would normally be tabled in this house. Therefore, in examining the achievements of this organization year by year, in order to ascertain what the three members have achieved and what might be expected through the addition of a fourth member, it would have been most helpful if we had before us the report of the harbours board. We find that in 1953 it was tabled on March 6. In 1954 it was tabled on March 17. We are now at the commencement of March of 1955. One would have hoped that we might have this report before us so that a number of the observations which are being made here today could have been confirmed by reference to the current report of the board. In opening this debate today the minister himself gave us figures which are now some 15 months old. They refer to the operations of 1953. Had he waited even a few days, perhaps he could have given us current figures and we could have seen the situation as it exists at present.
To return to the subject which has been touched on by several members, namely that of the local advisory council, may I say that my feeling is that, in certain of his remarks today and last week, the minister himself made the case that the board, with the addition of this member, cannot possibly fulfil the function of the local advisory council. Referring to the appointment both of this new member and other members, he pointed out that no matter from what region of Canada the man came, he would lose that local contact over a period of time as the result of his association with the board on a national level. If therefore the national harbours board, composed of three members, or of four members as is proposed in this bill,
National Harbours Board Act is a body which has the national point of view and if they are concerned with the national interest-and I am quite prepared to agree that they should be, and in the new appointment I hope that matter will be taken into consideration-then the point of view of the local area can only be advanced by a local advisory council charged with the interests of the local community and having no responsibility for the immediate problems of operation of the port as such, which problems are presumably adequately handled by the port manager. It would be an advisory committee without pay.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the national body-referring to this local situation-are much in the position of another group that I heard referred to at one time in these words: What they cannot understand themselves, they explain to one another. Even with the addition of this fourth member, the national body cannot understand adequately and sufficiently, because of lack of time, the problems of the local area. The addition of the fourth member-which I certainly am prepared to support and to encourage-will be a valuable asset to the operation of this board but it will not do away with the need for a local advisory committee or council.

I listened with a good deal of attention to the two members from Halifax who pointed out the valuable work that their local advisory committee had been doing, and certain things they mentioned are unquestionably applicable to some of our difficulties. My appeal in this respect is that the minister and the department should take the lead in seeing to it that a local advisory committee is established and recognized in our area. We more or less wonder who should be responsible, if not the minister, for the initiation of a local advisory committee. Should it be the municipal council of Burnaby? Should it be the city council of Port Moody? Should it be the longshoremen's union or should it be a particular shipping interest? In my opinion it is only logical to expect some leadership from the minister in this regard and I hope that he will give it.
The appointment of one member of the board from our area as well as the establishment of a local advisory committee would go a long way towards helping to solve some of the difficulties now confronting us and many of the difficulties that, with the rapid development of British Columbia, I am sure will face us. I should like to refer to the


statute, being chapter 187 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, which established the national harbours board and to read the description of the harbour of Vancouver from the schedule in order to indicate its size. It says:
For the purposes of this act, the harbour of Vancouver shall include Burrard inlet, with the Indian Arm, formerly known as the North Arm, and Port Moody, False creek and English bay-
I should like hon. members to take note of this part.
-and all other tidal waters lying east of a line drawn from the Point Atkinson lighthouse southerly to the most westerly point of Point Grey.
This area comprises some 60 or 70 miles of navigable waters. It includes such relatively distant places from Vancouver as Pitt lake, Pitt river and parts of the Fraser river that are not under the jurisdiction of the New Westminster local. It takes in the whole of Burrard inlet and Indian Arm. There is a great area there that eventually will be developed. In my opinion the expansion of harbour facilities ties in with such local problems as traffic congestion. Not many months ago we had a problem arise in connection with the unloading of heavy industrial machinery at the port of New Westminster. Long steel prefabricated structures had to be hauled through the main thoroughfare of New Westminster and other streets all the way up to Port Moody simply because New Westminster was the nearest unloading place available. A good deal of inconvenience was caused to the cities.
I believe that the harbour business is going to increase and that some attention should be paid to spreading out the facilities. In the city of Port Moody, which at one time had some harbour facilities, there is now established a $6 million pipe mill. That is no small undertaking, and I am sure it will have to make a good deal of use of harbour facilities. We have a chemical plant there as well as a large saw mill. In my riding we also have the largest saw mill in the British Empire. I understand they have to provide their own harbour facilities.
There is also another local difficulty that the minister's department will soon be faced with. I refer to the matter of a new bridge to replace the present drawbridge across the Pitt river. It is a dilapidated, utterly inadequate structure which needs to be replaced in the worst way. I am sure that as soon as the government of British Columbia has attended to the little matter of the Marpole bridge it will be tackling the Pitt river bridge and will be at the minister's doorstep asking him what he intends to do about it.
A local committee should also be at work to study what effect the St. Lawrence seaway

project is going to have on local employment and the shipping situation.

should like to say that in fixing these new rates we have endeavoured to maintain the proper relativity between the single and the married rates. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
we have listened with great interest to the remarks of the minister with reference to Bill 164. I think it was quite obvious to all hon. members, when the resolution preceding the bill was before the committee, that it was not meeting with approval. I am quite certain that the same disapproval which was felt then will continue to be felt, despite) the remarks of the minister this afternoon.
When we received the bill we found it disappointing. As I proceed this afternoon I hope to show in what ways it is disappointing to the war veterans across this country.
I believe it is fair criticism to say that the bill was introduced about three years too late. In 1952, in our veterans affairs committee, we urged that the war veterans

allowances be $60 for single veterans and $120 for a married veteran and his wife. We also recommended at that time that the ceilings be raised.
Neither of these things was done, although it was quite obvious to everyone that they should have been done at that time. When I say it is three years too late, we realize that in the three years that have passed many hundreds of war veterans in Canada have died. It would have been a great blessing to those men if they had had that extra allowance during the last years of their lives.
To get some idea of the number of men who have received help by war veterans allowances, I shall place some figures on record. Let me say at once that I think the War Veterans Allowance Act was one of the finest pieces of legislation ever enacted for the benefit of veterans. Between 1930 and 1954 there were 113,636 recipients of war veterans allowances. Since that time
72.149	have either been discontinued or have been cancelled. We realize of course that probably more than 90 per cent of these
72.149	are veterans who died since the bringing in of the act.
All one needs to do now, as has been done in the past, is to read each month the "Last Post" column in The Legionary to see that these men from the first war are passing away by the hundreds each month.
For a few moments this afternoon I should like briefly to go over the history to show why war veterans allowances were granted in the first instance. This is a long history, and I do not intend to give it in detail. I shall mention only some of the highlights and the important parts.
It all started back in 1927. Veterans hospitals, veterans doctors and veterans organizations such as the Canadian Legion became aware that there were many hundreds of men who had no disability that could be seen, and who were not qualified for pensions, but who were not able to carry on the ordinary procedures of looking after themselves and their family. Certain types of cases appeared for which no provision had been made in the existing legislation. The man who had been wounded and was suffering therefrom would be in receipt of a pension; but it was found that there were men who had served in a theatre of war who, upon coming home and trying to re-establish themselves, had found it impossible to do so. I might add that these men from the first war suffered far greater handicaps than those from the second.
In 1928 this matter was brought to the attention of the meeting of the dominion
War Veterans Allowance Act command of the Canadian Legion in the city of Saint John, and received wide publicity across Canada. The whole subject was brought to the attention of the people generally.
Dr. White, who was mayor of the city of Saint John and who welcomed the Legion to the meeting at that time, and was at the same time an outstanding doctor in Canada, and a man who had intimate knowledge of the conditions of these men, had this to say about them:
The war and its effects, the stress and the strain, the privations, the wants and the diseases, and all that he may have suffered while he was away have lessened his efficiency, have drained his vitality, which came about in three, four, five, six-yes, perhaps ten years and we find that a man, a robust man, with all his ambitions before him, which have been largely set aside on account of his patriotism now unable to carry on as he would have been had he remained at home.
That is the situation they found. At the time they said a man had aged 10 years. An hon. member said that here not long ago. I know it did not apply to every veteran who saw service in France, but it did apply to a great many men, because they are different constitutionally one from another. Other very able men took up the cudgels for this class at about this time. I mention the former minister, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). He was very sympathetic. He was at the Legion convention in Saint John at the time that Dr. White spoke. Sir Arthur Currie said that every man who experienced the hardships of war is paying some penalty. There was Brigadier General Alexander Ross, who spoke at the Legion convention at Calgary the next year. In his remarks he had this to say:
The most serious problem proved to be that of the broken-down or burnt-out veteran whose faculties were prematurely impaired but who suffered no apparent war disability as such.
Because he suffered no apparent war disability as such, he was not eligible to receive a pension of any kind.
In 1930 Colonel LaFleche, afterward Major General LaFleche, spoke as dominion president, and he had this to say:
The long and arduous years had changed the mental outlook of many men, as had the privations and hardships of war service ravaged their bodies and sapped their strength.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, that was over 25 years ago. The men we are dealing with today are 25 years older than the men who were mentioned at that time. Twenty-five years ago they were young men. They had earning capacity that the men who are living today do not have.
1734	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act I have mentioned these remarks ol men who brought about the war veterans allowance 25 years ago. I have done so, Mr. Speaker, for fear there may be in this country and possibly in this house people who still contend that we are wrong when we claim that the men-again I say not all of them- who are spoken of here were aged some 10 years by their service overseas and in the war. I should like to quote what the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., had to say a few weeks ago. His remarks are found at page 49 of Hansard, as follows:
A great deal ol nonsense has been talked about war veterans allowances.
I have been on committees of this House of Commons since 1935, and I think I can truthfully say that I have heard very little nonsense with reference to war veterans allowances. The hon. member went on:
The fact that it is an allowance for assistance and not a pension for a disability has seemingly been obscured and lost sight of.
I shall have something to say on that point in a few moments. Further on the hon. member said:
I was going to ask the hon. member for Esqui-malt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) to allow me to use him as an example.
Well, he was very unfortunate in his choice of an example when he picked out the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich because, as we all know, the harder the road the better he likes it, and the tougher the going the more he thrives. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich does not represent the type of man we are talking about here, the young man who was a clerk in a store or a young farmer who had no experience in roughing it. The service which they had to give in the trenches, going over the top and the great fear which everyone knows gripped the hearts of thousands of these young men did leave its mark. As I said a moment ago, these men I have mentioned and the thousands of people since and the millions of people in Canada who are in sympathy with this realize that a great debt is owed to them.
With reference to the argument that this allowance was for assistance and not a pension for disability, may I say that we all realize that was the original intention. There is no doubt about it that 25 years ago it was expected that these men would be able to supplement their war veterans allowance. It was also realized that they needed some help. The war veterans allowance has been raised from $20 to $30, to $50 and now to $60 for single veterans. I should like to quote, if I may, the remarks of Dr. Lumsden ex-president of the Canadian Legion, which fMr. Brooks.]	- - *	:

appeared in The Legionary of October 1953, with reference to this argument of subsistence. He had this to say:
Now much could be said in favour of the existing rates if it was the original intention of the War Veterans Allowance Act to give assistance and not subsistence.
At that time it was $40 for single men and $70 for married men. I continue:
For example, if it were regarded as assistance, then the man on a small pension-a pension of less than 50 per cent-could use war veterans allowance to bring him up to a minimum standard of living. The man on a retirement pension from the railroads, industry, et cetera, would be able to supplement his retirement allowance by war veterans allowance and so get by with a minimum standard of living, but that is not the way it now works.
And it is not the way it is going to work under this new bill the minister is sponsoring. I continue:
The maximum permissible income is so low that war veterans allowance itself must be regarded as the sole means of subsistence.	,
There is the point, Mr. Speaker. Dr. Lumsden goes on to tell how they were recommending $60 per month for a single man and $120 a month for a married man. Then he had this to say about permissible income:
The permissible ceiling on income is based too low, and so we have been pressing vigorously that this permissible ceiling be raised in order that the individual may supplement his war veterans allowance by pension, by retirement allowance if he has it, or it might be by steady employment, obviously of a submarginal standard and not enough to afford a living.
Because of the present ceiling, the war veteran cannot receive war veterans allowance and the old age pension, as we think he should.
The minister speaks about raising the permissible income. Permissible income has not been raised, Mr. Speaker. Under the old act, it was $120 for a single man. It still is $120 for a single man. Can you call that raising the ceiling? It is exactly the same. It is now $144 for the married man; it was $120. It has been raised around $2 a month. Before 1952 we had a permissible income of $250; now we have $144. It is practically the same as it was before. Certain veterans will be doing all right, and we are glad to see that. The single employable veteran is in a much better situation at $60 per month; there is no doubt about that. The employable veteran can take advantage of casual earnings, and I commend the minister and the department upon their definition of casual earnings and extending casual earnings so that a man will be able to earn an average of $50 a month. Also the single employable veteran can take advantage of section 4 of the act. The same applies to

the married veteran who is employable; he can take advantage of section 4 and also of the casual earnings.
The veteran who loses out is the man with a small pension. His pension and his war veterans allowance now have a ceiling beyond which he cannot go, and he may not be employable. The minister says there are a great many veterans who can take advantage of section 4 and do casual labour, but I believe that if a survey were made of those under the War Veterans Allowance Act it would be found that there are far more veterans who would not be able to take advantage of casual labour and section 4 than those who could. These are the men who are not getting the assistance they should get under a new act of this kind.
As I mentioned a moment ago, the veteran who is 70 years of age or over sees other men who have reached 70 years of age receiving as a right an old age pension of $40 per month, which interferes in no way with any other income they may be receiving by way of pension or from any other source. The older veteran under war veterans allowance may be living in a town with men who are worth $100,000, $500,000 or $1,000,000; yet he must exist on a paltry $60 a month while these other men have the full advantage of the $40 per month payment. That seems unfair to me, and I think it seems unfair to a great majority of the people in this country.
When this bill comes before the committee it is our intention to follow the same course we followed in 1952. At that time we asked that single men be given an allowance of $60, and this has been granted. We asked that married men be given $120, but they have been granted only $108. I am not finding the same fault with that as I am with the fact that no increase has been made in the permissible earnings. I have confidence that when Bill No. 164 comes from the committee it will not be in the same state. I have [DOT]confidence in the men who composed the committee last year and who I feel will be on the committee again this year. I remember members of the committee of last year and previous years stating time and time again that they were dissatisfied with the permissible income. This was said by members of the committee from all sides. If those bon. members are going to be consistent they will have to indicate their dissatisfaction with the permissible income which remains today just the same as it was last year, and which is lower than it was in 1952.
When the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) spoke the other day he said he was thrilled in 1954 when he was called back to his constituency to speak to
Income Tax Act
some irate veterans. If the hon. member does not ask for an increase in the ceiling on permissible income he is going to get another thrill when he goes back to Vancouver South after this bill has been through the committee. I am satisfied from what the hon. member said that he will support an increase in the permissible income under this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 163, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, because of the very short title which appears on this bill I have received a number of inquiries as to what it contains. Some of those inquiries appeared most hopeful, but I have had to reply that the really hopeful things that might be done by way of amending the Income Tax Act would have to be introduced by a minister of the crown. Much as I would like to be introducing a bill which would reduce the income taxes of those in the lower brackets or raise the exemption levels or take care of some other matters that need to be corrected in the Income Tax Act, as hon. members know it is not within the province of a private member to move such a bill.
This bill has as its purpose the lifting of some of the secrecy which surrounds corporation income tax matters as the act now stands. If I may use the language which I hear sometimes from some of my hon. friends to my right, the aim of this bill is to break through the veil of secrecy. I hope that certain hon. members like the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and others who appear most anxious to break through the veil of secrecy, particularly when crown corporations and public bodies of that type are being considered, will join with me in supporting this bill so we may break through the veil of secrecy with respect to corporation income tax matters, which after all are matters of public concern.
I wish to lay that down quite firmly, Mr. Speaker. The reason I differentiate in this bill between individual income tax returns and corporation income tax returns is that in the latter case there is always a public interest. Therefore I believe the public has a right to more information than it is now able to get regarding corporation income tax matters.

Income Tax Act
I should point out that my bill has two sections. Perhaps I might say that it has two parts or two propositions in order that I may refer to them without breaking the rule which says that one may not refer to the clauses of a bill on second reading. Actually my bill might be regarded as two bills rolled into one, having, therefore, two principles to both of which I must speak.
The first aim of the bill concerns hearings before the income tax appeal board. As hon. members know, there is a provision in the Income Tax Act which makes it possible for hearings before that board to be heard in camera, upon request. My proposal is that that section of the Income Tax Act should be amended to add the qualification that if the appellant is a corporation the appeal shall be heard in public. In other words, if that part of my bill becomes law it will still be possible for a private individual taking his case to the income tax appeal board to request that his appeal be heard in camera, but it would not be possible for a corporation to have its case before the income tax appeal board heard other than in public.
I think it has been an open secret that the incident which has prompted my interest and perhaps the interest of others in this proposal is the case covered by the income tax appeal board judgment No. 227, which concerned a certain firm which sought income tax deductibility with respect to some $27,789.02 which was spent for repairs and improvements to a certain property which it claimed it was using to entertain public officials in order to obtain contracts for government work. As hon. members know, the Department of National Revenue denied that claim in the first instance. The corporation in question thereupon appealed to the income tax appeal board, and in the end that board took the side of the Department of National Revenue and the deductibility was not allowed.

speechtext:
-to have a hearing of this kind in camera and enjoy the secrecy which has continued to surround the fact that it even tried to get income tax deductibility for an expenditure of this kind. Not only should it be taxed; we should know what firm it was.

The judgment of the income tax appeal board, signed by W. S. Fisher, a member of the board, had this to say:
I express no opinion as to why it should be necessary to entertain public officials in order to obtain contracts for work to be done for the benefit of public bodies, but apparently the appellant-and, no doubt, its competitors-have found that such entertainment has been not only necessary but also beneficial from a business point of view.
I suggest that this is a scathing indictment concerning the way in which some private businesses carry on. I suggest it opens up a very broad question as to whether there are any firms that are getting income tax deductibility for expenditures of that kind or for other expenditures which might have a political connection of one kind or another. It does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come to lift the veil of secrecy behind which matters of this kind are considered.
The hon. member for Eglinton and perhaps other hon. members in his party and some of us in this party have asked questions of the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Revenue a number of times, but to date we have not obtained much information about this firm or any dealings it may or may not have had with the federal government. Likewise, we do not know whether or not it had dealings with other governments.
I was interested in an article dealing with this matter which appeared in the February 12 issue of Saturday Night. This most interesting issue carried a picture of the Minister of National Revenue on the front cover, and on page 4 there appeared an article entitled "Tax Secrecy". After reporting the difficulties which I had experienced in obtaining an answer to some of my questions the article said:
Dr. McCann did not elaborate, but he should be questioned further. It might start a needed debate about the virtue of secrecy in cases that involve matters of public concern.
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the basis of this part of my bill. I feel that what is involved here and the whole matter which has been raised by Mr. Fisher's judgment is a matter of public concern. I suggest that the virtue of secrecy in cases such as this has been shattered, and that it is time we changed the law with respect to corporation hearings before the income tax appeal board.
Having raised the question of the appellant in case No. 227, I wish to say that I believe in the rule of law. I do not believe in changing the rules in the middle of the game, although I have seen that done. I do not think it is now proper to change the law in any retroactive way and deny to this firm the secrecy it enjoyed in that particular case.

Mind you, the government has the information. The government, through the Minister of National Revenue, was the respondent in the case and therefore must have all the information. It is up to the government whether or not it wishes to disclose the identity of the appellant. It is up to the government to decide what interpretation it places on the law with respect to that matter. The point I wish to make is that my bill does not try to change the rules with regard to the past. It is not unfair in that respect. It does propose, however, that the change should be made from here on and that in future no corporation should be allowed to go before the income tax appeal board in camera, in private, or behind the veil of secrecy.
I have been privately asked by some who are interested if there are not instances where individuals should not have the right to private hearings either. I have no doubt there are individual cases which might be borderline cases where secrecy should not be allowed. However, one has to lay down general rules, and I would say that there may be some individual cases which should not be denied the right to be heard in camera. Most individual cases should be accorded that right. Therefore the only way to deal with the matter is to leave it that all individual cases are covered by the provision that they can be heard in camera, on request.
On the other hand, so far as corporations are concerned, they are public bodies. What they do is a matter of public concern. I do not think they should ever have the right to take these appeals to the board and have them heard in camera. I hope those who have been concerned about the rather staggering or shocking revelations that came out of the appeal board consideration of case No. 227 will share my view that this is something not just to ask questions about, not just to make big speeches about on the floor of the House of Commons, but something to legislate about so it shall not happen again. On that basis I urge support of the first proposal contained in Bill No. 163, which is now before the house.
As I have already indicated, Mr. Speaker, my bill has two principles, two parts or two proposals. The other proposal is not new in terms of a public bill. It is a matter which I have laid before parliament on a number of occasions in the past. It is like some other matters that we fight for from this side of the house; we are obliged to keep on fighting for a long time until we win. I urge hon. members to think of this second aspect in the light of the things we have just been
Income Tax Act
discussing with regard to the judgment in case No. 227. Under that heading I drew the attention of hon. members to the fact that corporations are, after all, matters of public concern. What they do or how they carry on their business affects the economy of the nation. Not only does it affect the economy of the nation, but the revenues of the federal government are influenced largely by the arrangements-if I may call them that-that are made between the income tax branch and corporations that pay taxes.
Most individuals who pay taxes use the income tax form. It has been simplified. It is cut and dried and there is not much leeway as to what the tax will be. If you have the receipts for various allowable contributions or expenditures you get your deductions for them. If you have not the receipts you do not get the deductions. As I say, there is little leeway one way or the other as to the amount that, in the end, is paid by individuals.
In the case of corporations, however, there are many factors that are taken into consideration. There are such questions as allowances for depreciation and depletion. There is the question of the allowance for expenditures, what expenditures are necessary in the carrying on of the business and so on. We know that corporations retain legal counsel and accountants to work on these matters, and we know that many corporation income tax returns are the subject of claims and counterclaims between the corporation and the Department of National Revenue. However, the public does not know what the result is, although the public is affected by the amount of money that corporations, in the end, are required to pay-or are excused from paying-to the federal treasury.
I remind hon. members that on quite a number of occasions we have asked questions which I think were perfectly legitimate, the answers to which we have been denied on the ground that there is in the Income Tax Act section 133, which says that no information obtained from income tax returns can be given out. I think of occasions when there have been labour disputes, when the company or corporation involved has run huge advertisements ostensibly setting forth its side of the dispute but, in our view, castigating the workers unfairly. We have asked whether the cost of those advertisements would be allowed as an income tax deduction; or in other words was the public treasury paying for advertising of that kind. Every time we have asked that question-and I submit that it is a perfectly justifiable question-the answer given by the Minister of National Revenue has been that he could not give

Income Tax Act
that information because of section 133 of the Income Tax Act which provides for ironclad secrecy.
Similarly there have been times when we have felt that advertisements by chartered banks-even these harmless advertisements which nobody reads, setting out the annual report-have really been political documents. I have some on my desk-I shall not take time to read them-in which such comments are made that I do not think anyone would doubt that they are attacks on a certain political party in this country. Again we have asked whether the costs of political advertising of that kind are allowed income tax deductibility and we are met with the same reply, namely that this information cannot be given out by the minister because of the ironclad secrecy set out in section 133 of the Income Tax Act.
A few days ago-as a matter of fact, it was on the very day this bill of mine was introduced and given first reading-my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) presented a motion asking for certain correspondence exchanged between the government and certain corporations which he named. I am looking at a motion found at page 1331 of Hansard for February 21, 1955. This correspondence related to the question of tax liability and/or tax remission for the years 1946 to 1952 inclusive. My friend the hon. member for Dauphin has some information with regard to this matter which he obtained from government sources, and he may have something to say about it later.
The point I want to make here briefly is simply this. These corporations which were named by my colleague entered into certain negotiations or dealings with the federal Department of National Revenue which ended in a certain remission of tax even while the matter was still pending in the courts. I understand that this was done by order in council under the authority of the Financial Administration Act. I am not in a position to suggest that anything that was done was improper, but I suggest strongly that the public interest is involved and that we have the right to that information. When my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin proposed his motion on February 21, everyone knows what the reply was by the Minister of National Revenue, namely that he could not give this information because of the section in the Income Tax Act which surrounds income tax information, even though obtained from corporations, by this thick veil of secrecy.
I move on to another example, Mr. Speaker. Last session, on June 23, 1954, I drew the attention of the house to a rather fantastic

story, namely that of United Distillers Limited of Vancouver. As hon. members will recall, this is the case of a few men who were able to pyramid $4,000 into $20 million in a very short time by setting up certain corporations that were manufacturing and selling liquor just at the end of world war II. It really is a fantastic story, how they made the liquor in Canada, incorporated companies in Cuba and Panama and sold it in the United States, thereby making all kinds of money. Some of these people, including three Canadians, have been under indictment in the United States for evading the payment of some $16 million in income tax in that country.

I am not suggesting that we should swing the pendulum clear to the other extreme and start publishing huge books containing all the information the Department of National Revenue possesses, but I do submit that when members of parliament in the Senate or in the House of Commons on their responsibility as members feel that certain information regarding corporation income tax matters

should be brought out in the open, the minister at least should be free to give that information. That is all my bill asks for, so far as these matters are concerned, and I submit that there is not a member in the house who should refuse to agree to that proposition. 1 leave the section regarding secrecy in its present form and merely add these words:
Provided that nothing in this section shall operate to prevent a minister of the crown from communicating to the Senate or to the House of Commons any information with respect to corporations obtained under the provisions of this act.
As I have already pointed out several times, the bill makes no change in the strict secrecy provisions that now apply to income tax matters so far as individuals are concerned. That is true both with respect to the right to be heard in camera before the income tax appeal board if you are an individual, and with respect to information contained in individual income tax returns. But I strongly urge that the time has come for a new look at the whole picture so far as corporations are concerned.
I have noticed some of the editorial comment criticizing this bill even before it has been debated in the house, and I do not mind that. In fact, I am glad to see it, and to know what are the arguments against the bill. For example, the Financial Times a while ago pleaded that a corporation is an entity and, as such, is entitled to all the rights and privileges accorded the individual. But I notice when we advocate that certain matters should be publicly or socially owned one of the stock replies is that corporations today are publicly and socially owned, that they are owned by the people. It is said that they are not private entities unto themselves, but that they are part of the warp and woof of the economy we have today. I suggest to these people that they cannot have it both ways. If private corporations, so-called, are really publicly owned, in the sense that the people of this country own them through their ownership of shares and so on, and if they play the part that the apologists of private enterprise say they play in building up the economy and in paying money into the federal treasury, then I submit that makes them clearly a matter of public concern, and that they should not be allowed to hide behind this veil of secrecy which is found in the act.
It has been there a long time, I know. It is one of the traditions of the income tax legislation in this country, and it is hard to break it down. But I submit to hon. members who are annoyed by the veil of secrecy with respect to some other matters that here is a place where one should start to pierce the veil.

I invite hon. members to give serious consideration to both aspects of the bill, and I would remind them that it does simply two things. First, it provides that future hearings before the income tax appeal board would always have to be in public when the appellant is a corporation, so that no firm could hide behind secrecy with respect to any Shangri-La, or the like. Second this bill asks that the secrecy clause regarding information obtained by (the income tax branch be modified so that it would be possible for a minister to give information to the Senate and the House of Commons, particularly when asked for by members of the Senate or of the House of Commons on their responsibilities as servants of the public, in their pursuit of the best interests of this country as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the bill, and do so because I believe there is a definite public interest to be protected in this matter.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made reference to a certain return I attempted to have passed by the house on February 21. The reply given at that time by the Minister of National Revenue, in refusing to bring down the return, was that the secrecy provisions of the act would prevent his doing so.
I am not questioning that reply or the position he took, because if the act does not permit his making public certain information, then of course he is bound by the act, just the same as anybody else. But there have been some serious doubts in the public mind as to the basis upon which certain decisions were arrived at, particularly as they referred to corporations.
Today I should like to bring to the attention of the house one particular case in which I feel there is room for considerable doubt, and where the decision reached calls for an explanation by the government. That was the reason I asked for the return. I wanted to know on what basis the government arrived at the decision which they made valid by order in council, and what were the factors which led them to believe they were making a good deal for the treasury.
The return for which I had asked had to do with certain tax remissions made by the government, by orders in council, to a group of companies. The companies concerned were the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, the Gatineau Power Company, the Saguenay Power Company Limited and the Bell Telephone Company.
So no one will think I am singling them out for any particular reason I would refer hon. members to part II of the Public Accounts, at page 4 of which they will find a statement as required by the Financial Administration Act, which sets out
the total list of companies receiving tax remissions. There are a few other than the ones to which I have referred, but these four happen to be the larger ones. A large amount of money was involved, and it was for that reason I wanted to have all the facts.
My first question asked whether these particular firms received any tax remissions for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, and there was an affirmative reply. The amounts of the remissions given were as follows: The Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, $549,697.68; the Gatineau Power Company, $496,772.60; the Saguenay Power Company Limited, $576,598.15 and the Bell Telephone Company, $371,659.68. That adds up to almost $2 million. Naturally any citizen of Canada who is a taxpayer and who looks through the public accounts would want to know why these companies should receive tax remissions amounting to almost $2 million, particularly those who have been harried and pursued by income tax inspectors in recent years, and those who are wondering what is going to happen to them this year. For example, only yesterday the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson) asked the Minister of National Revenue whether the government was going to allow any leniency to those who suffered crop failures in the west when it comes to the collection of income tax. Part of his question reads as follows, as found at page 1677 of Hansard:
Can the minister assure the house that the practice of garnisheeing entire bank accounts which are required for spring work operations will be discontinued?
The minister replied:
I can give no such assurance.
I have a particular case in mind where the equipment of a farmer has been garnisheed by the government in order to collect the tax they claim is due. Very little consideration was shown as to whether or not that person was in a position to pay. But if a harried taxpayer looks into the public accounts and finds that four Canadian companies have had remission of taxes amounting to close to $2 million, he will want to know why. It was for that reason I sought the information. The only information I was able to get was contained in the return of Monday, February 14, 1955, sessional paper 99-B. The explanation given to my inquiry as to why these remissions were made is as follows:
In 1946, the legislature of the province of Quebec imposed a tax, known as the Quebec education tax, on certain companies.
Among them were the four to which I have made reference. The return continues:
In computing the federal tax liability of the companies in question for the years 1946 to 1952,

Income Tax Act
this tax was not allowed as a deduction for the purpose of establishing net taxable income.
That was interesting to me. I looked up the statutes and I found that the authority for the non-allowance of the deduction is contained in section 12, paragraph (g) of the act, which reads as follows:
A corporation tax, as defined by regulation, paid to the government of a province or to a municipality, or-
That was included as one of the deductions not to be made for income tax purposes. Quite clearly this was a tax paid to a provincial government. The result was that the matter was submitted to the income tax appeal board, presumably by the companies concerned, and the board decided in favour of the companies. Then the government took the matter to the exchequer court as an appeal, and the board's decision was reversed.
The important thing to remember is that the only instance in which a court ruling was obtained was that of the exchequer court, and that court ruled in favour of the government. In other words it ruled that that tax could not be deducted, and that the companies had to pay their income tax as assessed.
The next step was that the companies concerned appealed the decision to the Supreme Court of Canada. Before the appeals were heard by the supreme court the government introduced an amendment to the act. They amended that section of the act by providing for the deletion of paragraph (g). The amendment reads as follows:
Subsection (1) of section 12 of the said act is amended by inserting the word "or" at the end of paragraph (f) thereof and by repealing paragraph (g) thereof.
That was to be effective from January 1, 1953, and for subsequent taxation years. In other words they removed the paragraph which provided that certain deductions such as I have described could not be made, and the amendment was to apply to 1953 and subsequent years. In other words, by no stretch of the imagination could it have any effect whatever on the tax liability of those companies for the period 1946 to 1952, which was then in question before the supreme court.
But what happened next? Those companies approached the government. There is no information to show whom they approached or whom they met over there, but the government of course has to take the responsibility. I read again from the return of February 14:
The companies in question, prior to the hearing of the appeals by the Supreme Court of Canada and subsequent to the passing of the above-mentioned legislation-
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
The legislation referred to is the amendment which removed paragraph (g) of section 12. I continue:
.-made an offer to settle the appeals on the basis that they be allowed, as a deduction in computing their taxable income, one half of the amounts of the Quebec education tax paid by them in respect of each of the years 1946 to 1952, inclusive.
It is a very interesting situation. The exchequer court had already ruled in favour of the government, that the companies were liable for a certain tax. The companies took their appeal to the supreme court, but before the appeal was heard in the supreme court the government amended the act to make it possible to make such deductions from 1953 on. On that basis, they received an offer from the companies concerned to pay half their liability and let the rest go. There is something very fishy about an approach of that kind. What was the reaction of the government? I read again from the return:
Taking into consideration the uncertainty of the outcome of the pending appeals to the supreme court-
I see no particular reason why there should be any great uncertainty in the mind of the government, when one considers that the exchequer court had ruled in its favour. Apparently, the government had very little confidence in the good judgment of the exchequer court. I continue:
*-and of the effect of the new legislation, it was considered advisable to accept the offer of the settlement made by the companies.
The second part of their reason or excuse is very interesting. They say "taking into consideration the effect of the new legislation". What was the new legislation? It was the amendment to section 12, which was to take effect in 1953 and subsequent years, and which had absolutely nothing to do with the taxation years 1946 to 1952. The government had absolutely no grounds for speaking about the effect of an amendment passed in 1953 which plainly stated it was to take effect in that year and in subsequent years only. It was not retroactive. They had no reason to believe that legislation would have any bearing on the dispute between the government and the companies in the years 1946 to 1952. On that alleged basis the government allowed a cash remission to these four companies amounting to almost $2 million.
There should be no surprise that the government did that. Hon. members and the public generally should feel very suspicious about that kind of deal. Certainly the grounds on which the government claims those tax remissions were made appear to be very fishy. Here we had a court ruling, the only one up to date, in favour of the treasury.

An appeal was taken to the supreme court by the companies. Certainly the government would have every reason to believe that it the exchequer court had ruled in its favour, and if the legislation which was on the statute books until 1953 was sound, it could have relied on the judgments of the courts rather than on the shaky premise outlined in this return in which they say:
Taking into consideration the uncertainty of the outcome of the pending appeals to the supreme court and of the effect of the new legislation-

I shall be glad to do that. In order to place clearly before the house why I was objecting to the secrecy provisions contained in the act it was necessary for me to refer to particular cases and go into some detail. I have covered that ground now, and would go on to point out that clearly there is a legitimate reason for the citizens of Canada feeling doubtful and even suspicious when tax remissions amounting to almost $2 million are made to four companies on a basis which does not appear to be well-founded. When we attempt in this house, as I did on February 21 last, to obtain copies of the correspondence between these companies and the government dealing with the tax dispute, we are met with a refusal.
I should like to point out that in this proposed return I was not seeking information as to the financial position of these companies, or as to anything contained in their income tax returns. I was simply asking for the correspondence between the government and the companies with respect to the dispute, and that is so stated in the question. That was refused on the grounds of this secrecy provision.
If this house and the public are ever to get the full story behind this deal, which after all involves $2 million which in my opinion should have gone into the public treasury; if they are going to be able to judge whether the government used good judgment and had sound reasons for accepting the deal, which on its face to me looks very shady and suspicious, the only way we can make that judgment, the only way we can satisfy our minds that everything was aboveboard and at arm's
length, is by getting copies of the correspondence and finding out what transpired. As it is now, as soon as we get near the source of information the curtain is rung down in our faces and we are told, "Sorry, boys, we just simply cannot tell you what took place. It was a deal which cost the public treasury $2 million, but we cannot tell you just how it was arrived at."
Individual taxpayers, including farmers, wage earners and others, are finding these days that the screws are being tightened by the collection branch of the Department of National Revenue, and stiffer treatment is being handed out at a time when there is a great deal of hardship in some parts of the country, when they will not take "no" for an answer, or even "maybe". At such a time the government are able to make a tax remission of $2 million to four companies and not explain the situation in this house, make no attempt to justify it; and when questions are asked they tell us they cannot give us any information because of the secrecy provisions of the act.
Under circumstances of that kind I believe that all hon. members of this house, whether they sit in opposition or on the government side, as individual private members representing the taxpayers and the citizens of Canada have a right to demand that the veil of secrecy be removed; that where there is reason to believe that something of an unusual nature has been done by the government by order in council the full facts should be placed before this house so everybody will be satisfied that the taxpayers and citizens of Canada are receiving justice at the hands of this government.
