The hon. member had this to say in describing that meeting, as recorded at page 101 of Hansard of January 11, 1955:
I had to do some very frank talking.
I am certain the hon. member had to do some frank talking indeed.
I had to tell them that, so far as we on this side of the house were concerned-and I was sure it was also true of others in all parts of the house-
That was a very generous statement coming from the hon. member.
-we would continue to do our level best to see that those in Canada entitled to war veterans allowances got their just due at the earliest possible moment.
As I see it, the earliest possible moment at which the war veterans will get their just due will be when the committee on veterans affairs is set up and the matter is placed before it. The hon. member was very generous in saying-
-so iar as we on this side of the house were concerned-and I was sure it was also true of others in all parts of the house-
-considering the fact that we on this side of the house have been pressing not only this year and last year but for a number of years for what we consider, and I think the veterans and the public consider, to be the just due of the war veterans, and considering the fact that the war veterans have not received their just due entirely because of the members on the other side of the house. That statement does sound rather peculiar to me, and I am sure it must also seem peculiar to other hon. members.
I could mention many other hon. members, but I do not wish to do so at the present time. Time and time again the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode), the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Mac-Dougall), and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) have intimated that this permissive income was too low.
The minister mentioned the fact that the female veterans, the widows of veterans and others would be included under section 4 of this bill. We highly approve of that. It certainly is a move in the right direction. This is a point which has never been given the consideration by the veterans which we expected. I was quite surprised to read in
(Mr. Brooks.]

the last report issued by the Department of Veterans Affairs that in round figures only 1,100 veterans out of approximately 30,000 had taken advantage of section 4. This was the case last year and I have no doubt the figures have increased for this year.
We need not be surprised at that because, as I mentioned this afternoon, the veterans are becoming too old. Today the average age of the war veteran under veterans allowance would be about 64 or 65. These men are getting too old for casual labour or to take advantage of section 4 of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
The minister also mentioned-and of course it is in the bill-that there will be an increase in the salaries of the board in charge of war veterans allowances. We can see no objection to this provision. Increases in salaries have been given in the Department of Veterans Affairs and every other department composed of men who have practically the same positions as these men in charge of war veterans allowances. I have always felt, and I have no hesitation in saying this, that these men have done and are doing a good job. I feel also that the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the department have been very fortunate in the calibre of men they have had administering the act.
There are some things which are not in the act which I would like to have seen included. For instance, I would like to have seen allowances granted to the men who required them who had service in England during the first war. This is an old recommendation. I have heard this recommended in this house for the past 15 or 20 years. There are very few of those men alive today compared with the number a few years ago. While we cannot use the same argument for them, that is that they were aged by service in France, I still think the same argument could be used as was used for the men under the dual service.
It seems to me that when we are bringing this act up to date we should give consideration to those men who had service only in England. Service in England during the second world war was considered as service in a theatre of war. Despite the fact that conditions were more dangerous in England during the second world war than during the first, England was nevertheless bombed in the first war, and the men who served in the first division in England were encamped at Salisbury plain and other parts of England and their accommodation did not equal that provided in the second war.
There is another matter which has been brought before veterans affairs committees on many occasions. I refer to the widows of

allied veterans. Under the act as it stands at present imperial or allied veterans who have had 20 years' residence in Canada come under the War Veterans Allowance Act, but their widows do not unless these men have had that 20 years' residence. The result is that an allied veteran might have 19 years and 360 days' residence in Canada and lack only a few days' residence to qualify his widow for receipt of the war veterans allowance should he die before those few days are up.
It has been recommended, and I think it is a reasonable recommendation, that if the widow has had 20 years' residence in Canada she should then be entitled to the allowance if her husband would have been entitled to it if he had lived here for 20 years. I think that is a most reasonable request. The widows of our Canadian war veterans allowance recipients and those who are entitled to it receive it when they reach the age of 55. I think there should be an amendment to the act to provide that these widows of imperial and other veterans should receive the war veterans allowance on reaching the age of 55, if resident in Canada for 20 years.
Mr. Speaker, this war veterans allowance has been given first consideration by the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans, the army, navy and air force veterans, the amputations association, the war blinded association and the war widows. All these people have considered that war veterans allowance should have first priority in veterans affairs during the last few years. The one thing they have been most critical of has been the ceiling on war veterans allowance or the amount of permissible income.
A few years ago-I think it was in 1951, as I remember it-the Pension Act was before the veterans affairs committee. The committee of that day did not consider that the increase in pensions was large enough. It was only 10 per cent. It was scorned by the members of the committee and by members on all sides of the house. Representations were made, and an offer was made to increase it to 15 per cent. That figure was not acceptable to the committee. It was brought up to 25 per cent. Some of us thought it should be more, and recommended 33J per cent. But it was generally agreed that 25 per cent would be accepted, and the committee made that recommendation.
As to this Bill No. 164, I am satisfied that the members of the committee from all sides of the house are again going to feel that justice is not being done to the veterans. I am satisfied that Bill No. 164 will be amended just as the pension bill was amended a few years ago.
War Veterans Allowance Act
In. speaking this afternoon the minister rather compared the recipients of war veterans allowance with those who were ijn receipt of pension. I did not follow his argument, and I should like to read more carefully what he said; but in my opinion you cannot compare war veterans allowance recipients and those in receipt of pension. With regard to those in receipt of pension there is no ceiling on what they can earn or what they may receive outside of their pension. They may receive $1,000, $10,000 $15,000 or whatever they are able to earn whatever their income may be.

Mr. Speaker, this bill will be before the committee. There are many other points we can discuss at that time. I may say I am pleased indeed that a veterans affairs committee is being set up. Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the minister and the explanations he gave for the government's action in introducing this bill as it now stands. I must admit that when listening to the minister, one has to be extremely careful indeed not to permit the genial atmosphere which he creates to affect one's judgment. I shall have to read carefully tomorrow what he has had to say today in order to be quite certain that I understood correctly the information he gave us.
I also listened with a great deal of interest to the historical review of the war veterans allowance legislation given by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and to his speech in general. There is one thing to be noted about this sort of legislation, Mr. Speaker. We may be in different parties and we may

War Veterans Allowance Act question one another's judgment on certain things, but on this side of the house-and I know it is true with regard to a good many members on the other side of the house- when it comes to a question of veterans legislation, there is a common sympathy for their problems.
In the explanatory notes we find this:
The principal purposes of the amendments are to provide for an increase in the present monthly allowance and for the raising of the limits of the permissible income, and to extend certain benefits of the act to certain additional classes of persons.
We in this group support the principle of the bill. The criticism we have is that there is not enough of the principle. We are pleased indeed that the government has introduced the bill and has at least gone part way in meeting the requests of the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations and the needs of large numbers of veterans and their dependents. But we in this group are sorry they have not gone all the way in meeting the needs of the people we are concerned about this evening. Many veterans and their dependents, the members of this house and the veterans organizations in Canada have been waiting for three years for this legislation. You, Mr. Speaker, can readily appreciate the fact that, even- with all these faults in the bill, we are glad the government has seen fit to act to this extent.
When we come to deal with this type of legislation I cannot help thinking of my former comrades, and I know other members in this house think of their former comrades on these occasions. I notice the honourable and gallant member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) is listening intently. I am pleased to see that, because I know he is interested in this question. In fairness, Mr. Speaker, I may say that while I question the hon. member's judgment on occasion, I have a great respect for his excellent war record.
Mr. Speaker, I said I thought of my former comrades who will be affected by this legislation. Many of them will benefit to some extent and others, because of the limitations of the legislation, will not have their present circumstances improved. At this moment I am thinking of a man who was in our company. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) knows him well. I refer to Jimmy Hall of Graham's landing who during an advance captured, single-handed, a German commander and a whole brigade staff. He entered a German dugout on our right flank unexpectedly. When he walked down the steps he found a brigade staff. The German commander said, "Who are you?". He said, "I belong to the Kootenay Cougars" and they all surrendered immediately. That
[Mr. Herridge.l
man saved a number of lives in our battalion on that occasion by the capture of that commander and his staff. He did great work that day for Canada, single-handed, for which he was decorated. He returned to Canada. He has worked hard since then- until last year, part of the time for the government of Canada. However, he is getting on in years; he cannot quite take it any longer. He now receives war veterans allowance. He has been thrifty and hard-working. He has saved a little bit. He has been a good citizen.
That is the type of man I am thinking of tonight when I plead for increases in war veterans allowances and improvements in the bill. I can think of another man whom the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra also knows because we served together in the same company. His name is Joseph Crowell, who lives in my home town and was a scout in our battalion. He went through the most unusual experiences and his health has suffered ever since on account of those experiences. He also was decorated for bravery. He worked up until the last year or two, and he is now on war veterans allowance. He has had an invalid wife to take care of for over 15 years. He has had to get along on an allowance of $90 a month, look after an invalid wife, and at 75 years of age look for the odd job to keep him going. These are the men of whom I am thinking tonight when I support improvements in this legislation.
I can think of a man from the native town of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, Tom Horner. We went through some interesting experiences together during one of our raids at Ypres. He is now in Shaughnessy hospital, not suffering from a pensionable disability but from a physical breakdown, without doubt occasioned by his exceptional and unusual war experiences. In my personal recollections I think of Reggie Howe, the secretary of our 54th battalion regimental association of which I have the honour to be the honorary president. He has also suffered for many years from disabilities and ill health. These are the kind of men, and their dependents, whom I am thinking of when I ask for improvements in the war veterans allowance legislation.
This legislation is of great importance, as we all know, to many veterans and their dependents, and because of that has been of great concern to the Canadian Legion, particularly during the past three years. To support that I want to read briefly from the report of the resolutions committee at the

last convention of the Canadian Legion. The paragraph is entitled "War Veterans Allowance" and reads as follows:
Before we submit our resolutions in regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act, we feel that a few preliminary words of explanation are due to the delegates of this convention.
Then there is the heading "Importance of Matter". It continues:
The importance of this matter is indicated by the number of recipients of war veterans allowance across Canada and by the acuteness of their need. At present there are approximately 42,000 veterans who are receiving some assistance under this act. There are many thousands more who are in need but under existing legislation are not eligible for the help they require. If anything is to be done to help these people it must be done soon, and we would seek to impress upon the delegates to this convention the fact that there is no matter of veterans legislation of greater or more immediate concern to the veterans of Canada than that of war veterans allowance. It is imperative that we do what we can and do it quickly.
The next paragraph is headed "The Legion's Role", and reads:
For years we have been pressing for an increase in the allowance, the raising of the permissive ceiling, and a broadening of the basis of eligibility. Some progress has been made in legislation and amending of regulations, which has eased the problems of those able to do light work. But little has been accomplished for those who are unable to work. There is not much we can do in the way of presenting suggestions for new legislation or for the development of new arguments for positions already established. The current Legion thinking along these lines has been crystallized in the brief submitted to the cabinet in November of 1953 and we do not see how we can go much beyond that.
Further progress must depend upon the ability of the local branches to convince their federal members that this matter is of primary concern and that we insist on immediate action. Dominion command must give direction and aid in the development of such a campaign, but the ultimate responsibility must rest on the branches, and success or failure will depend upon their ability to convince their M.P.'s both of the justice of their cause and of their determination to see that action is taken.
I read that to illustrate the great concern of the membership of the Canadian Legion with this problem. I am sure that the introduction of the bill, as I said before, will be welcomed by the members of that organization. There is no question about that. While we criticize it as not going sufficiently far, the bill will bring comfort to the hearts of many veterans and their dependents; but we on this side of the house think that unfortunately it overlooks many others. The bill meets the proposals of the Canadian Legion with respect to the allowance so far as single veterans are concerned. It will be of considerable assistance to married recipients of the war veterans allowance.
We wish the proposals of the Canadian Legion had been met in full. We cannot understand why the government did not go
War Veterans Allowance Act the whole way and meet the requests of the Legion when it decided to go as far as it did. However, we are pleased with the improvements that have been made. Our main criticism concerns the failure of the government to raise the ceilings on permissive income. I think that is a valid and sound criticism, and will be the criticism of veterans organizations when they make their representations to the committee.
Under the old plan a single veteran received $50 a month, and his total income could be $720 a year. Under the new plan he will receive $60 a month and his total income must not exceed $840 a year. So far as the single veteran is concerned that means there is no increase in the ceiling on permissive income above the allowance. We in this group think that is a great mistake. The government is losing the opportunity to assist many of these veterans who would like the ceiling raised along the lines of the proposal of the Canadian Legion. Even if the government could not see their way clear to go that far we think they should have gone much farther than they have in the bill.
With respect to married veterans, under the old plan a married recipient received $90 a month and his total income could not exceed $1,200 a year. Under the new plan he is to receive $108 a month, quite a substantial improvement, but his total income must not exceed $1,440 a year. So far as raising the ceiling on permissive income for married recipients of war veterans allowance is concerned, such a man now has the magnificent extra and additional sum of $2 a month allowed with which to improve his standard of living.
I think the government can be soundly criticized for not going further than that. I know the minister mentioned that the cost of the changes proposed in the bill will be somewhere between $9 and $9i million. We know that is a large sum of money, and we in this group recognize the fact that we have a responsibility to the taxpayers as a whole. But we think there is such a thing as relativity. I admit that raising the permissive income would mean an additional expense of possibly several million dollars, but when we consider that we are expending some $4,000 million a year I do not think it can be said that we are unreasonable when we ask for a few extra millions to be expended on war veterans allowances to provide for the old age of men who protected and defended this country, particularly in the first world war, while in many cases others made substantial profits and fat livings.
An increase in the ceilings on permissive income would be of material assistance to

There is no question about it; it has been of great assistance to many veterans. I think personally it was an excellent definition of casual earnings, quite fair and generous. We recognize that. Further than that, I am willing to compliment the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs who have been responsible for administering that definition of casual earnings. I think they have been most fair, and most anxious to do for veterans all that the law and the regulations permit.
But while that new definition of casual earnings has been of considerable advantage to many veterans, it has not helped a good many others. I believe that in failing to raise the permissive income the government has failed to think of those who cannot work, whose health is such that they are unable to undertake any employment, even of a casual nature. The income of those people is confined strictly to what they receive as war veterans allowance.
In addition there are those who have some tiny regular income, either from earnings or from some other source. Under the definition of casual earnings even today, as I understand it, if a veteran has a job, we will say in a hospital at $20 a month the year round, that is not classified as casual earnings. Those are our main criticisms of the bill. Our first criticism is that we think the government should have gone all the way, so far as payments to married recipients of war veterans allowances are concerned. They should have met the proposal of the Canadian Legion. Then, second, they should have at least gone further than they have in the matter of permissive income. The other amendments to the act, which make provision for a small group who to date have been overlooked, are welcomed. I am sure they will be of great value to what I understand to be the relatively small number who will be affected.
Before concluding I wish to make two further suggestions. Like the hon. member for Royal, we in this group wish the government would introduce amendments to the act so that veterans of world war I who served in Great Britain would come under its terms. As the hon. member pointed out, these veterans are few in number; the number is growing less every day. But I know of cases of men who served in various posts in Great Britain, and did so quite unwillingly. Indeed there were several such men in my own battalion, and I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will bear me out in this. When we got to England they were sent to London or to the north of Scotland or somewhere else to do a job, and were not allowed to go to France. Because of the decision made by their military superiors which resulted in their continuing to give their service in England or in Scotland, they are now denied the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act. I do think it is about time we brought those veterans of the first world war who had to serve in that fashion under the terms of the act.
Then I believe recipients of war veterans allowances who have to leave Canada because of their health should receive the allowance while they are out of Canada. We allow judges and other pensioners, as well as pensioned civil servants, to go to the West Indies or anywhere they wish. There is no restriction on their residence. But I know of several cases where men have had to go to other countries for health reasons, on the recommendation of their doctors, and while absent from Canada they lose their war veterans allowance and can only receive it for three months upon their return. That is three months' allowance is retained for them until they come back.

I know of a case in my own constituency of a man who was on war veterans allowance for some years, and who suffered from a serious non-service chest disturbance. I met him on the street a good many times, and his lung condition was so bad that his breathing reminded me of a horse with the heaves. He has gone to Shaughnessy hospital repeatedly, and they can do nothing for him. They have done the best they could, and may I say I have the highest regard for the services rendered by the officials and the staff at Shaughnessy hospital. Upon seeing his doctor again he was advised to try Mexico. Two months ago he left Canada and is now residing in Mexico City. I am not sure of the medical term describing his malady, but I do know he has benefited by the altitude and dryness of the climate there. He can now breathe with reasonable comfort, and life is more comfortable and happier for him because of that.
When a veteran who has served his country finds it necessary, on the advice of his doctor, to live outside Canada under circumstances such as I have described, we should allow that veteran to receive war veterans allowance while it is necessary for him to remain outside the country.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Lest I be accused of delaying this measure I shall make my remarks as brief as possible. However, I do think that one of the important functions of parliament is to have proper and thorough discussion of whatever comes before it.
I listened with considerable interest to the Minister of Veterans Affairs this afternoon, and I felt rather sorry for him because I am satisfied that he was not expressing his own personal opinion. I believe that if it had

War Veterans Allowance Act been left to him personally we would have had a little more complete legislation than we have before us at this time. Throughout his whole speech there was one conclusion I was able to draw, namely that there is a vast difference between veterans allowances and veterans disability pensions. I sometimes wonder why this should be so. However, I shall have more to say about that later.
Mention was made of the fact that the new scales of subsistence benefits that are allowed under clause 4 will assure "a reasonable standard of existence" for the veterans. I wonder whether that is all these veterans, who gave so much of their lives to the service of this country, are entitled to. I can recall recruiting meetings before the first war when we pledged to these people that they would be looked after completely by the country for which they were willing to offer their lives.
Another thing I notice is that allowances are under constant study, and that need for revision upward will be under consideration. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how many of these veterans will have passed to the great beyond before this upward revision takes place. It is a sad state of affairs that while those people are suffering and are being forced to exist on what, on our own admission, is merely a subsistence level, they should continue to suffer while we wait to see if we can do something better for them.
I was also glad to know that the definition of casual earnings is being widened. The thing I would just like to ask this house to consider is what stability is there for the veteran if he has to resort to casual earnings. Those veterans are entitled to a degree of stability when one takes into consideration what they have done for us in years gone by. But the worst slap of all, Mr. Speaker, is that when those veterans reach the age of eligibility for the old age pension, that pension becomes deductible from their war veterans allowances.
We have been told that to increase the permissible income would cost approximately $5 million. When we speak of $5 million it does sound like a lot of money. But when you stop to think that $5 million is little more than one-tenth of 1 per cent of our total budget it does not sound like a very large amount, does it? It represents one package of cigarettes per person per year in Canada.
I was rather surprised by the optimism of the hon. member for Royal. He is hoping that good will come out of the study of this bill in committee. I hope he is right. I am sure there will be members in that committee who will press for the revision we are asking for, but I am afraid I am not quite as


optimistic as he is. However, we wish him luck. I know there will be various members on that committee who will do their best to have the injustices removed.
The hon. member for Royal dealt very well with all the extra assistance and what might be called the statistics of the bill. Therefore I shall pass that up. I should like this house to realize that we are dealing with the welfare of over 45,000 men and women. We are not critical to the nth degree of this bill. We are gratified to see it brought before the house.
While we are gratified, I must say that we are not satisfied. Our firm belief is that when a veteran has established a need for an allowance he should be entitled to the same consideration as the veteran who was disabled on the field of battle. I cannot see why there should be distinction. It is quite possible that the effects of his service in the years gone by have not shown up until this day; but if he had been disabled on the field of battle of course he would have been entitled to a pension which we know and admit is the finest in the world today. But we cannot see why there should be this great difference between the war veterans who become prematurely aged or through some other physical or mental disability are unable to earn their living in the later years of their lives, and others.
Of course we know there is no ceiling implied whatever with respect to the veteran on disability pension, and that is as it should be. We are not speaking against that, but we cannot see why this discrimination applies to war veterans who are perhaps just as disabled as others who are drawing similar pensions because of battlefield disability. We know the Legion recognizes that there should be a ceiling in accordance with the income tax regulations, but I should like to see- and I think I am speaking for every member in this group when I say this-the ceiling entirely removed.
Let the Department of National Revenue look after that; they can make a good job of it. Why should there be a ceiling against those war veterans?
There are many regulations affecting the money that is paid to these veterans. I refer now to what is commonly spoken of as perquisites. A veteran may have a few chickens producing a few eggs, or a cow to supply milk for his family; or he may go out in the bush to cut his own wood and thereby get exercise that is good for him. But the veteran is penalized for all these things. This is something else which I trust will be taken into consideration when this bill is before the committee.

In closing I would merely say, let us treat our burnt-out and prematurely aged veterans with the same consideration we show to the disabled veterans. Let us show the prematurely aged veterans that we realize that they did their best for Canada, that they sacrificed their health and several years of their lives on the altar of service. Let us treat them with fairness and not with discrimination.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to enter this debate after eleven o'clock this morning, when I was hit with the 'flu bug; but there are a few things I would like to say. First of all I want to congratulate most sincerely the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the government for bringing in this legislation which in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of all those on this side who have spoken on this bill, is definitely a step which will be appreciated by the recipients of war veterans allowances from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I should like to indicate my appreciation to the hon. member for Royal who referred so kindly to the various members of the veterans affairs committee and their willingness to press the government for additional increases in connection with this type of legislation. I think I can say safely that no matter how excellent this legislation might be my good friends to my left would still find a million and one reasons for criticism. None of us ever gets in life exactly what he wants, and I do not think any hon. member of this house would expect to find in a bill brought down by the administration that it was like Scotch whisky, ne plus ultra, and no one could find any objections to it.
There is no question but that improvements could be made in this bill. However, we have gone a long way, and I would draw that to the attention of the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod). He stated that many things were promised to the volunteers in the first world war. I happen to be one of those, and to be candid I was never promised a damned, solitary, single thing. Over and above that the members of the first Canadian expeditionary force did not ask any questions as to whether they were going to be pensioned or whether they were going to be nursed in military hospitals in Canada should they come back wounded. They went over there without any promises and did as good a job as any Canadian could be expected to do on any battlefield.
I am not for one moment endeavouring to detract from the desire of hon. members to my left to see perfection. All of us would like to see perfection. I can assure the house that as far as the recipients of war veterans 50433-1 IN
War Veterans Allowance Act allowances from east to west and at all intervening points are concerned, this legislation is going to be greatly appreciated. Make no mistake about that.
The previous speaker referred to the widows of imperial veterans not getting a break because some of them had been in this country for 19 years and 360 days. That is too bad; I am sorry about that, but I think it should be looked at in a practical way, in precisely the same way as matters were looked at by the members of the committee which brought about the recognition of universal old age security. It was realized that there must be a line of demarcation between those who are eligible and those who are not eligible. Our security legislation requires 20 years' continuous residence. What about the poor older man or woman who has been here only 19 years and 360 days? Those who fall within that bracket are going to have to wait just as the widow of the imperial war veteran, referred to by the previous speaker, will have to wait. All people like this will be deprived of legislative benefits until they are here for the necessary period of 20 years.
We must be fair and realize that rules must be laid down to differentiate between those who are eligible and those who are not eligible. That is all that is being done by this bill. We might in a most affable way wipe out everything, but make no mistake, there are a great many members of the Legion who still believe that as far as certain types of legislation are concerned the means test, if you wish to call it that, is still necessary.
I had one in my office yesterday. When I listened to my good friend the hon. member for Kootenay West I wondered, if the Kootenay Cougars were the fighting hounds from hades that he made them out to be, how the first world war ever lasted four years.

I think we had a pretty good fighting aggregation. There were over 15,000 casualties who had come through to that body as reinforcements, but we never thought we were that good. When we gathered back here in Canada after the war to talk things over we always referred to ourselves as the fighting 46th, which never took a trench but never lost one. There seems to be a difference of viewpoint as between the Kootenay Cougars and the South Saskatchewan fighting 46th.
I cannot agree or go along with my good friend from Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) when he says that in his opinion there should be no differentiation between the recipients of war veterans allowances

War Veterans Allowance Act and recipients of disability pensions. I do not think that is quite a fair statement. My good friend from Vancouver-Quadra said something like "tsk, tsk".

speechtext: No, I did not say it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
He says he did not say it, but he was thinking it. Well, it is possibly better that my good friend from Vancouver-Quadra thinks quietly rather than out loud. However, I think there is a definite reason for having the line of demarcation drawn between those who were disabled on the field of battle and those who are the recipients of war veterans allowances and who served possibly only in the United Kingdom.
I know those of us who were on active service during the first world war thought it was pretty posh to get a bit of a leave so we could go to the old country. It was a great treat and a far cry from eating rice out of a sandbag in France. To be able to lie in a hutment in the United Kingdom was a far cry from lying on your ground sheet half submerged in water in a shell hole. I need not draw your attention to these things. Certainly there was a great deal more physical suffering and hardship in the front echelons in France and Belgium than there was in the reserve areas back in the United Kingdom. Because of that difference I think it is both fair and monumentally justified for the administration to make that distinction between the two types of service.
It is true, as one of the previous speakers has said, that with the disability pension there is no ceiling on your income as such. There is no argument about that. But in the same breath I wish to tell you that many of those veterans who are in receipt of disability pensions have never been able to earn the amount of money the war veterans allowance recipients have earned.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has said, and I agree, that we have the finest type of veterans legislation in the world. I shall not be quite as extravagant as he was in describing who brought it about, but with all deference to the Canadian Legion and the various provincial commands I do say that had it not been for the spirit of the government down through the years in granting additional benefits to both disability pensioners and war veterans allowance recipients, the work of the Legion by itself would have come to naught, as a Yorkshire man would say.
Consequently it has been not only the Canadian Legion and the members of parliament but the members of the government as well, from the first world war up to the present, who have made this veterans charter the thing of which we as Canadians are


intensely proud. We in this house took great pride in watching the veterans charter grow and develop from its infancy. When I enlisted in the first world war I received no promises as to what I would get if I went overseas. I think one of the main reasons I joined up was because I got only 51 per cent in my last Latin examination the year before, and so I enlisted. Believe you me, I was scared to death of the second one coming up in the fall.

We should realize that no one, whether or not he is a member of this house, ever achieves all the things about which he dreams, and he never attains the ideal toward which he shoots. Somewhere along the line, however, there is the great factor of common interest which has as its basis and objective the desire for the betterment of conditions this year over what they were in previous years. In my humble opinion the reception afforded this legislation by the veterans of Canada will be extremely joyful. It is not going to be the end of the trail; I do not think the government anticipates that it will be what Harry Lauder used to describe as "the end of the r-r-road." Certainly, however, it is a great step forward and will accomplish something over and above what we had last year or the year before.
In conclusion I again congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and I also include his parliamentary assistant who, I know, is a strenuous worker. I also congratulate the government generally, and certainly I wish to include my good friends to my right regardless of their political affiliations. Those I have mentioned, and the Legion and the government, have taken steps for which we are extremely thankful to benefit those who have fought for us and made freedom possible in our day.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
I enjoyed listening to the hon. member who has just finished. He said one thing with which I agree, that those who went overseas in the first Canadian division during the first world war were promised nothing and expected nothing. They gave their service to our country freely, voluntarily and without having been coaxed. Those men who returned are today asking for assistance and the legislation we are considering tonight concerns them.
For that reason I consider this to be an important bill. I feel I must indicate my disappointment concerning this bill because it does not meet the demands set forth by the

Canadian Legion for the benefit of our older citizens and their families. This bill concerns and greatly affects the standard of living and happiness of many of the most patriotic citizens in this country.
While I express disappointment because I do not think it goes far enough, nevertheless I do not want to leave the impression that, generally speaking, our veterans have not been fairly well used. I think that on the whole they have been well treated. I should like to say now, because I think it is fair to say it, that under the veterans charter and the subsequent legislation our Canadian veterans have been and are being well looked after.
I want to congratulate the personnel of all branches of the Department of Veterans Affairs for the sincere and able manner in which the administration of this act is carried out. In particular I want to draw the attention of the minister to the fact-and I want him to know this-that those connected in any way with veterans affairs in my province of New Brunswick are doing a splendid job on behalf of our veterans. I know many of them through having had a good deal to do with veterans' claims, adjustments and hospitalization over the last nine years. One could not ask for or expect more courtesy or interest than has been shown in any case which I have had the pleasure of discussing with departmental officials during the past few years.
I also think it fair to state that I have found those officials who are particularly interested in the administration of the war veterans allowance claims to be not only efficient but sincere. I have found that they will go all out to do everything possible, within the act and the regulations, to assist these older veterans. I am speaking from the experience I have had, and I am sure many other hon. members in this house have had the same experience. I think the personnel of the Department of Veterans Affairs deserve to have this credit given to them by those of us in the house who have had the privilege of working with them.
I also think that the public should realize, as oftentimes they do not, that these officials are trying to do everything they can for the veterans. But the officials of the department, whose duty it is to carry out the administration of the act, are bound by the act; the scope of the act is limited by the legislation which we pass in parliament and by the regulations that are laid down by the government. I therefore sometimes do not appreciate hearing some of my good friends the
War Veterans Allowance Act veterans and others criticizing the departmental officials when, in reality, it is those who are higher up the ladder who should be criticized. It is our responsibility.
That is why I am taking a few minutes of the time of the house tonight. I feel that it is up to us, while we are at it, to try to do at least a fair job on this legislation. I realize that a good case has already been made out. Those hon. members who have already spoken have, in reality, said about all that needs to be said in order to impress upon the government that they should go a little bit further. However, I am going to add these few words in the hope that the minister and the government may be brought to the realization-not in particular by what I say but by the preponderance of our cumulative effort to impress this upon them-that they are now making a mistake in not making the limits of permissible income really fair.
I am not going to take any time to discuss the increase in the payments. It seems to me to be fair, but I think the ceiling on the permissive income should have been brought in line at least with the present exemptions allowed under the Income Tax Act. If the government does not feel that it could go as far as the Legion asked in the case of the single person, I think it should have considered-and maybe it will-the amount which is allowed under the income tax as an exemption. I think that is about the minimum that is considered should be left with a person to get along on and live on. They are entitled to that amount at least before they contribute anything directly to the federal treasury. Anything less than that for these old patriotic citizens is, in my opinion, less than fair.
I am sure that the 20 per cent increase will be appreciated, though I think it will be found that old married couples will feel that they have not been quite fairly treated, when comparison is made with the treatment given to a single person. It seems to me they will think they are not getting equivalent rates. I believe the lowering of the age limit of the female veterans and the widows is going to be appreciated.
I do not wish to take up much of the time of this house, and I have little more to say; but I believe the case for the veterans is one that should not be passed over lightly. I believe this committee is going to take a good look at this legislation. I believe they are going to come back with some recommendations to increase this ceiling of permissive earnings. I hope that they will receive a sympathetic reception from the government. For once I do not think it

War Veterans Allowance Act would hurt the government to admit that they may have made a mistake, or that they had not considered this matter sufficiently.
I believe the permissive income ceiling should be raised at least some. When you come to think of it, while you are giving a married couple a 20 per cent raise, $1,440 a year does not begin to allow a couple who have no other assets to live decently. As has been said, it is true that many of these veterans have homes. They may not be good ones, but at least they have a place to live. They have no rent to pay, and they are good homes so far as they are concerned.
But there are others who have no place to live. They must rent. I think those veterans should not only be able to get this allowance but should be allowed to earn enough to rent a decent place in which to live. I am sure that each and every hon. member in this house tonight can think of veterans in his own constituency living in rented quarters which neither you nor I, Mr. Speaker, would like to see our father and mother live in. They are compelled to live in those quarters. They have not the earning capacity to go out and earn money. They must depend upon the war veterans allowance. They might mow a few lawns and do a little bit of work of some kind to increase their income. The wife might baby sit. There are many things, but when they are confined to $240 they cannot do very much and a total income of $1,440 will not go very far.
As I said before, I think the matter has been very well covered, much more ably than I can do it, and I would only be wasting time by continuing. I concur in the many statements and arguments that have been put forward by various speakers. I am sure the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations, from whom I have been receiving letters for the last three weeks, will be disappointed if the government do not reconsider the matter, recant and at least raise the ceilings on permissive income.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure my very good friend, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Jones), that I shall give him plenty of opportunity in just a moment, because I do not want to unduly delay the house. From the spirit of the speeches so far I know that members of all parties are


anxious to get the bill through this stage as soon as is reasonably possible and send it to the committee.
I must say that as a member of the committee last year it was a very great pleasure to me to see that no matter how fiercely we felt called upon at times to carry on our party battles, we all seemed to get together on the substance of what was right for the veterans. Some members of the house will recall that I ventured to predict we would find ways and means of bringing this whole matter to a head within a very few months, and that is precisely the way it has worked out.
I particularly want to speak tonight in support and praise of the minister's action in bringing in these changes this year, because even from this side of the house I felt called upon on my last day here last session to be sharply critical of the government for not having made changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act in that session. As the hon. member for Royal has pointed out, I made some reference to going back to an indignation meeting that had been called in my own riding. Incidentally, I may be wrong but I believe my riding has more veterans than any other riding in the whole of Canada. At least I think I have the most vociferous.
But I want to correct the hon. member for Royal in one respect. On that particular night they were not talking of raising ceilings; they were too busy raising the roof. Personally I am very well pleased with the progress we have made so far, and may I say that I do not believe for a minute that this legislation represents the ultimate in veterans benefits in this great Dominion of Canada. The whole history of veterans legislation in Canada is that we have improved it almost ever since we had any veterans legislation. I can remember the history of our veterans legislation for a great many years, because I happen to have been writing for' Canadian newspapers for 33 years without a break, and in that time I have had a good deal to do, one way and another, with veterans legislation.
I cannot say that I altogether agree with the historical memories of my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall), when he says there were no promises made to the veterans of the first world war. I can remember the then prime minister of Canada, Sir Robert Borden, saying to our Canadian army overseas, "When you come back, Canada will be yours". I can remember the prime minister of Great Britain telling the servicemen in that same war how he was out to make England a land fit for heroes to live in. As I remember those times there were many promises made to those who served in all armies, and very specific promises as to general benefits.

We can remember that when this country pioneered the war veterans allowances-I think it is true that no other country has any legislation comparable to our War Veterans Allowance Act-we started on quite a modest level; but as years went by the legislation became more generous and more generous, as some might say, but let us say more just and more just. I think all of us were highly gratified and satisfied when even in this year of considerable financial difficulties the government saw fit to make an exception to the general curtailment of expenditure and bring in a really far-reaching advance with respect to the scores of thousands of men who served Canada in time of need.
I am going to be very frank with the house tonight. I would of course like to get up here tonight and say that I think the government should have raised the ceilings on permissive income to $1,200 and $2,000. Of course I would like it better if the government, in addition to raising the cash payments from $50 to $60 a month for single veterans and from $90 to $108 a month for married recipients, had raised the ceilings to $1,200 and $2,000 a year instead of to $840 and $1,440, although according to my arithmetic these are substantial cash raises indeed in the ceilings. I ventured to point out to the house last year that perhaps we could hope for a cash increase of $5 a month with an increase in the permissive ceiling to $1,080 a year, which would have meant that a veteran on attaining the age of eligibility for old age security could have received the full $40 without any deduction.
When I went back to my own constituency and actually faced the hundreds of people who are very much concerned with this question I was asked by some of them for my honest to goodness opinion about what the veterans might get by way of an increase, in the light of what the government was up against in the way of balancing the budget and so on. I said that I thought they might get $5 a month cash raise and that the ceiling might be boosted to $1,080 a year. However, those veterans, without any exception, immediately protested to me in the strongest possible terms and told me to forget all about an increase in the permissive ceilings, that what they wanted was the largest increase in the cash grant they could get. They said that if they had to choose between a $5 a month cash increase and a permissive ceiling of $1,080 or a $10 a month cash increase and very little change in the permissive ceiling they were all for the cash raise of $10 a month, because the vast majority of them are the kind of people who are not worried
War Veterans Allowance Act about the extra permissive income for the simple reason that they have no extra income at any time.
Therefore I want to say that while I personally fully intend to continue, over the months and years, to do my modest bit to see that the war veterans of Canada, their wives, their widows and their dependents get the best possible break from the country,
I would not want to leave any shadow of a suggestion that I think there will be any substantial change by way of raising the ceilings on permissive income in the veterans affairs committee.
I shall tell you why I think that; because I think the minister who has had to pilot this bill through the cabinet, and who has had to convince treasury board in a difficult period that the country should stand a certain extra financial contribution, has done a pretty fair and workmanlike job, and every honest man and woman in this house should really take off his or her hat to him, because he has done that good job.
I would say the same of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to whom last year I had the privilege of passing on the sum and substance of many hundreds of letters of protest I received from war veterans in my constituency. In many cases they enclosed detailed budgets, right down to the last penny, showing the great difficulty they were having to stay alive on what they were then receiving.
I will say that because the government saw fit to yield to the suggestions that were made, not only by myself but by a good many people on all sides of the house, I certainly intend to give my loyal support to the program this government has come out with this year, because I think it is a pretty good instalment to work on.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the last speaker was speaking for himself and not for the government when he said he expected that the committee would not deal with the permissive income ceiling. Because if that is the case, and if the door is already shut, then we need not call the committee together at all.
I also take issue with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard when he tries to draw a line of demarcation between the war veteran who receives an allowance and the veteran who receives a disability allowance. The payment of a burnt-out pension to a veteran is a distinct medical and physical disability payment; make no mistake about that. I think the late Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie made that quite clear in the early stages of the proposal to bring this payment about, when he said these people were definitely victims of

War Veterans Allowance Act the war-physically or mentally or in many other ways-and that therefore they should be taken care of in the same way as a man who lost an arm or a leg. In many cases, while they have no scars on their bodies they have them in their hearts and minds. It was the recognition of this fact by the government that made the veterans allowance possible in the first place.
It has been scientifically and medically proven that any veteran who had active service overseas in either war suffered physical deterioration to such an extent that it could be considered that ten years of his life had been taken away from him. For this reason I take exception to anyone trying to create a line of demarcation between the two disabilities. They are the same, and should be treated in the same way. The burnt-out veteran should have the same privileges, and should have the same lack of ceiling that is enjoyed by the disability veteran.
In spite of that, however, I think this bill will be welcomed by every veteran in Canada. It will be especially gratifying to those members of the Canadian Legion who have worked so hard for years to convince the government that this bill is necessary and essential. I do feel, however, that the permissive income should have been increased at least to the modest sum suggested by the Canadian Legion. It may be that during the passage of the bill through the committee stage the minister can change his mind and increase the allowable income.
I received today the last edition of The Legionary, and find that their comments on this bill are quite fair. They say in a heading: "At last: W.V.A. Increases" and in another heading "Good, but not Enough". Their chief complaint is summed up in this paragraph:
The increase from $1,200 to only $1,440 in the total permissible income for married recipients and from $720 to only $840 for single men should also be reconsidered. Many of these aging veterans, while incapable of taking steady jobs, can do part-time work and thus augment their incomes. It seems unreasonable to deny them the right to help themselves, if able to do so, to achieve something in their declining years which at least approaches a decent standard of living; and it surely cannot be argued that this can be attained on $840 or $1,440 a year with living costs being what they are.
I think in that paragraph The Legionary has stated the case better than I could, so I shall leave it at that. While this bill also makes provision for the widows and children of veterans, it does not provide for all the widows and all the children of veterans who have died in the service of their country. That is why I wish to make one more suggestion for the inclusion of another clause in the bill to take care of that situation.

The minister has already shown a willingness to try to alleviate the distress caused directly or indirectly through service, and this loophole to which I have drawn attention should be attended to. I shall give a specific case that is now before the Department of National Defence. It is the case of a young soldier who volunteered to serve in the Canadian forces, and was sent to Germany. He was there three years, and while there naturally made German friends. One week end he was invited to go to the home of some friends. These German people met him at the camp and took him to their home. On the way back to the camp they met with an accident in which this soldier was killed.
I have tried to get some recognition for his widow and her children. True, he was off duty at the time of his death; true, he was driving with a German civilian. Through the Department of National Defence the government has promised to take legal action against the driver. That was a year ago, but that action has not yet started, and I do not know when it will start. The case is getting colder and colder all the time, and becomes more difficult to handle. Meantime the young widow and her two children are living in my constituency. They cannot obtain any pension whatever.
The sore point, to my mind, is the fact that if he had served in the army for ten years the widow and children would have qualified for pension. Why should there be this ten-year provision? I claim that if a soldier serves for only a day he becomes the responsibility of the government. I would ask the minister to remove that provision so that it would carry the restriction for only one year or, better still, have it removed entirely, so this widow would be cared for.
The fact is that the husband was in the service when he was killed. Once a man enlists he loses all contact with other sources of income, and becomes the servant of the government. His whole life is placed at the service of his country. Therefore I claim the government is morally responsible for this soldier's welfare, and it is also responsible for his family in anything it may suffer as a result of that service. This should apply from the date of his enlistment.
To cover a case such as I have mentioned and hundreds of other borderline cases, as they might be called, that are not covered by the present act, assistance being given only on a social-service basis or by a provincial government, I suggest that the minister should begin a new system whereby every member of the armed forces immediately upon joining the service would be covered by a $20,000 insurance policy. This

policy would cover him in the event of illness, accident or death, whether on or off duty. In that event a widow such as I have described would not be left at the mercy of charity.
Such a policy definitely would encourage enlistment, and would provide protection in such cases as the one I have mentioned. I believe these insurance policies can be bought fairly reasonably, payable in full in 15 years. This paid up policy could then be given to the soldier on leaving the service. It would give him immediately some security that he has missed through lack of contact with civil life, and he could start anew in the new world he has to face. Otherwise he is left with no economic security through having sacrificed the best period of his life in the service of his country. In order to protect him and give him something worth while for having done so, the least we can do is to present him with a $20,000 paid-up policy at the end of his service.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
I rise chiefly on account of what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. He did not seem to be aware of the fact that the war veterans allowance is paid only in recognition of service in a theatre of actual warfare. Unless you had service in a theatre of actual warfare you cannot get the war veterans allowance. War veterans allowance is not a general service pension; yet the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard talked about the disability pension being paid for service in France or in a theatre of actual war, while the war veterans allowance was being paid for service in England.
In so far as the first war is concerned, it is just the other way around. The war veterans allowance can be paid only if the veteran had been to France. On the other hand, the disability pension could be paid for service in England. The disability pension could be paid for service even in Canada provided the disability was incurred on duty or even off duty, because we had the insurance principle at that time. It is very important to keep in mind that the war veterans allowance is paid in recognition of service in a theatre of actual warfare, and England was not a theatre of actual warfare in world war I. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard was talking about service in world war I.
The two main grievances up to this session were the amount of the allowance and the ceiling. The bill before us makes quite a substantial increase in the allowance, but there will be wide dissatisfaction with the ceiling. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South that of the two the amount 50433-112
War Veterans Allowance Act of the allowance is the more important. If we cannot get as far as we want to go in both directions, then it is a good thing to get the farthest in regard to the allowance.
I say that because the man we have to look after first of all is the man who is practically totally disabled and has no other source of income. To him the raising of the ceiling is of no use. On the other hand, the more you can raise the allowance the more that man will benefit. I have in mind veterans who are practically totally disabled who, because of certain limitations within the Pension Act, are not able to qualify for a pension. For instance, there are men who are disabled today, but owing to the fact that their disability was classified as of preenlistment origin they are not able to qualify for a pension. Therefore as a last resort they obtain war veterans allowance.
So far as that benefit is concerned, of course the greater the allowance the better. So far as the ceiling is concerned, it makes no difference to them. Therefore I congratulate the government on having gone so far as they have in so far as the allowance is concerned. They have reached the objective of the Legion with respect to the single veteran, but they are still $12 short in so far as the married veteran is concerned. The minister pointed out that the assistance fund would raise it another $12, but I do not know of any single veteran who is getting it. Some are getting it, but it just so happens that the only veterans I have knowledge of are not getting any assistance from the fund. I take it that assistance is given chiefly in the cities, and we do not find it so much in the country.
There is one matter that I hope the minister will give further consideration to, namely the widow of the imperial veteran. An imperial veteran who resides in this country 20 years qualifies for war veterans allowance, but if he dies one day before he has been in this country for 20 years his wife is not eligible for a pension. The government could very well say that so long as the widow has resided in this country for 20 years she shall qualify. I understand that it would not affect a very large number; therefore I do hope that the minister will give further consideration to that point.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to participate in the debate because, although this bill is going to the veterans committee and will return to the house, this is the better opportunity for those of us interested in this problem who are not on that committee to have something to say about it.
At the resolution stage of this legislation I made some criticism with regard to the proposal the minister was bringing down. Now that we have the bill before us I see no reason to withdraw any of that criticism. The issue is becoming a bit confused with regard to war veterans allowances, owing to some of the things that have been said by the minister, and some of the things that were said tonight by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, perhaps unintentionally on his part; I do not know. He left the impression with me, as was just mentioned by the hon. member who took his seat, that war veterans allowance was payable to those who were not in a theatre of war. Of course he was quite wrong.
Confusion arises in the minds of many people in regard to this matter. In order to qualify under the act a veteran has to be 60 years of age, unless there are exceptional circumstances; he has to have had service overseas in a theatre of war, and be unable to carry on his normal duties. He may be able to do intermittent work but not able to carry on his normal duties, and he has to be unemployed.
The type of person who qualifies for this allowance is a man who is really in difficult circumstances. That should be kept clearly in mind when we are discussing this problem. Second, let us keep clearly in our minds that these men with service in a theatre of war in many instances endured just as much as the men who suffered in other ways and have since been receiving disability pensions-not that anybody wanted to suffer in that way overseas. It is well known to all veterans that many of our disability pensioners, through ill luck on their first trip to the line or their first battle, saw very little service in that theatre of war.
On the other hand this group of people on war veterans allowance include a number of men who served overseas for lengthy periods.


The hon. member for Kootenay West gave us two or three good examples of that. I well recall when I was in France serving under two sergeants, both of whom had reached that theatre of war in 1915. They had undertaken every trip into the lines, they had been engaged in every action in which the first division participated, and both of them lasted until September, 1918, when unfortunately one was killed. The other survived until the end of the war and was with the army of occupation in Germany. Think of the length of service involved in the case of that survivor, from 1915 right to the end of the war.
It should be remembered that in that war living conditions were extremely grim. Leave was a scarce article indeed. If a man got leave from a theatre of war to England once in the course of 12 months he considered himself lucky. There were many men like that who suffered from exposure to the elements as well as from the actual strain of warfare.
Our medical friends tell us that does have its effect on people. I have no medical knowledge, but I have seen men who were shellshocked immediately on going into action, without any previous experience in that connection. In the second war this was called battle exhaustion. A man could become battle exhausted with no more than five hours of service. Shell-shock resulted in what appeared to a layman as a complete collapse of the nervous system, and some seemed more subject to it than others. It is just possible that in the course of years, even though a man recovered from such an experience, he might suffer a disability which could not be shown to make him eligible for pension.
Anyone who had that experience overseas in the first world war needs no convincing as to what men should qualify for war veterans allowances. These men served their country well. They were the ones who lived in the trenches. A total of 400,000 Canadians got to France in the first world war, of whom 60,000 were killed, practically all in France. A total of 180,000 were wounded, which left about 160,000 who got to France but were not wounded. The chances of escaping were not very good. Of that 160,000 only a small portion would have served in the rear areas, and even there during the first world war there were bombing attacks as well as shellings by long range artillery.
I think of the men who are the recipients of war veterans allowances as being men who served long periods overseas without being wounded. Many of them have now reached the age of 60 years and require assistance. I believe a grateful country will give them that assistance without worrying too much about it. Niggardly ideas enter into the

minds of those who are drafting new regulations or new bills in order to accommodate themselves to the situation. I do not think the people of Canada generally want anything in the way of small treatment given to men of these types. As I have been trying to point out, and other hon. members also, these men served and suffered from exposure as well as danger.
The number of those receiving war veterans allowances is not very great. What complicates the matter is that we now have some coming under war veterans allowance who served in world war II, and then there are the widows and orphans to be considered. But taking those who served in world war I or in earlier wars like the South African war or the northwest field force, we find the total in round numbers to be 21,000 who are over 60 years of age. Those under 60 years of age total 4,000 in round numbers.
As the hon. member for Royal pointed out, they have been disappearing rather rapidly. The hon. member gave the totals of those who had been on war veterans allowance from the beginning, and showed the decrease which had occurred. It works out at about 3,000 a year. If you examine the figures for the last five years you will find that the number of recipients of war veterans allowance from world war I has been staying approximately at 25,000. Those who are given awards or are reinstated are balanced by those who
Business of the House are cancelled or who have been suspended, and the cancellations would include those who have died. So the burden is not an increasing one. As the years go by it is going to decrease.
